title: Smartwatch “heart arrhythmias” alert leads to a diagnosis of PAC-induced cardiomyopathy in a 34-year-old man; ablation lifts his ejection fraction from 15% to 50%
summary: Göttingen: a smartwatch alert in an asymptomatic 34-year-old revealed frequent premature atrial contractions and LVEF 35%, later 15%; radiofrequency ablation restored LVEF to 50% at six months.
account: Soubh, Rasenack, Haarmann, Zabel and Bergau reported a case in European Heart Journal - Case Reports. The authors are at the Department of Cardiology and Pneumology, University Medical Center Göttingen, Germany. It was published 15 April 2025. The event dates are not given. A 34-year-old man with no medical history consulted his primary care physician. His smartwatch had detected “heart arrhythmias” while he was asymptomatic. A 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) showed sinus rhythm with frequent premature atrial contractions (PACs). A cardiologist found a left ventricular ejection fraction of 35% with a dilated ventricle. Despite guideline-directed heart-failure therapy he returned months later with palpitations and chest pain. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed LVEF 15%. Coronary disease was excluded by computed tomography (CT) angiography. Holter recordings showed a PAC burden of 30–50%. High-density 3D mapping located the ectopic focus at the left inferior pulmonary vein. Radiofrequency ablation terminated the arrhythmia. At six months he was symptom-free with LVEF 50% and fewer than 1% PACs. Spironolactone was stopped. The authors call it the first reported PAC-related arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy initially detected by a wearable. The watch's brand, model and the form of its alert are not stated.
purpose: Smartwatch arrhythmia alerts are built to prompt medical review of irregular rhythms. The alert here served that purpose. The condition it uncovered, PAC-induced cardiomyopathy, is one the authors say wearables are not usually credited with finding.
system: Smartwatch arrhythmia detection (brand and model not stated)
developer: Not stated (the report does not name the device's maker)

ratings.reason: The alert started a chain that diagnosed a cardiomyopathy. The condition progressed to LVEF 15%. Ablation reversed it to LVEF 50% with resolution of symptoms. The authors present early detection as what allowed the heart failure to be treated before further progression.

ai_role.statement: The watch's detection of “heart arrhythmias” is what sent an asymptomatic man to his doctor. Everything after (ECG, echo, MRI, mapping, ablation) was clinical. The report does not say what the watch flagged, whether a notification or an ECG reading, nor which algorithm. The device's contribution is therefore established only as the trigger.

fields.account: Soubh, Rasenack, Haarmann, Zabel and Bergau reported a case in European Heart Journal - Case Reports. The authors are at the Department of Cardiology and Pneumology, University Medical Center Göttingen, Germany. It was published 15 April 2025. The event dates are not given. A 34-year-old man with no medical history consulted his primary care physician. His smartwatch had detected “heart arrhythmias” while he was asymptomatic. A 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) showed sinus rhythm with frequent premature atrial contractions (PACs). A cardiologist found a left ventricular ejection fraction of 35% with a dilated ventricle. Despite guideline-directed heart-failure therapy he returned months later with palpitations and chest pain. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed LVEF 15%. Coronary disease was excluded by computed tomography (CT) angiography. Holter recordings showed a PAC burden of 30–50%. High-density 3D mapping located the ectopic focus at the left inferior pulmonary vein. Radiofrequency ablation terminated the arrhythmia. At six months he was symptom-free with LVEF 50% and fewer than 1% PACs. Spironolactone was stopped. The authors call it the first reported PAC-related arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy initially detected by a wearable. The watch's brand, model and the form of its alert are not stated.
